title: Interpret an A/B test with a segment reversal
prompt:
A teammate says "Variant B won, ship it." Using only the table below, explain in at most
170 words whether that conclusion holds and what you would do next.

Checkout conversion by device:

| Device  | Variant A              | Variant B              |
|---------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Desktop | 400 of 2,000 (20.0%)   | 1,440 of 8,000 (18.0%) |
| Mobile  | 640 of 8,000 (8.0%)    | 120 of 2,000 (6.0%)    |
| Total   | 1,040 of 10,000 (10.4%)| 1,560 of 10,000 (15.6%)|
system:
You are completing one task from an evaluation suite. Do the task as asked.

Reply with the requested text only, with no preamble about what you are doing.

rubric.name: spots_reversal
rubric.description: States that A beats B within both desktop and mobile even though B leads in the total, and concludes that 'B won' does not hold.

rubric.name: explains_mix
rubric.description: Explains why: the variants received very different device mixes (B mostly desktop, A mostly mobile) and desktop converts better, so the total reflects the mix. Naming Simpson's paradox is optional.

rubric.name: next_step
rubric.description: Recommends a sound next step: do not ship B on this evidence; investigate the unbalanced assignment and rerun or compare within device.

rubric.name: accurate_and_brief
rubric.description: At most 170 words and every number quoted matches the table. No invented statistics.

reference:
The conclusion does not hold. B has the higher overall rate (15.6% against 10.4%), but A
converts better on both devices: 20.0% against 18.0% on desktop and 8.0% against 6.0% on
mobile.

The total is misleading because the two variants saw different traffic. B's visitors were
80% desktop and A's were 80% mobile, and desktop converts far better than mobile for
either variant. B's overall lead comes from that mix, not from the variant itself. This is
Simpson's paradox.

It also means the assignment was not properly randomized, or it was broken by device, so
the test itself is suspect.

Next: do not ship B. Find out why the device split differs between the arms, fix the
assignment, and rerun the test with a balanced split, then compare within each device. On
the current evidence, A is the better variant.
answers:
Yes, the conclusion holds. Variant B converted 15.6% of visitors compared with 10.4% for
Variant A, which is a 50% relative lift on a sample of 10,000 users per arm. That is a very
large sample, so the result is clearly statistically significant. B did slightly worse in
each device row, but those are smaller subgroups and the overall number is the one that
matters for the business. I would ship B to 100% of traffic and keep monitoring the
conversion dashboard for a week or two to confirm that the improvement holds up in
production.
